title: Terminal-Register Certification for Finite-Measurement Learning of Multiscale Quantum States
authors: Bhvain Makwana, Kashyap Patel, Manjunath Joshi, Jaideep Mulherkar
abstract: Structured quantum-state learning not only depends on an expressive ansatz but also on an operational certificate that stays meaningful with finite measurements and imperfect implementation. We study pure one dimensional states learning by an inverse binary multiscale entanglement renormalization ansatz (MERA). In the learning procedure, the qubits removed during coarse graining are controlled coherently and measured together at the terminal register. We confirm that an ideal sequential and terminal measurement schedule delivers the same complete bit string distribution under matched causal operations, while normalized postselection can amplify perturbations inversely with prefix acceptance. A noise aware theorem introduces an individual calibrated total variation implementation budget to the finite shot certificate. The protocol is estimated on an open boundary transverse field Ising ground state. A frozen 8-qubit schedule using $560$ million simulated training measurements per run achieves fidelity above $0.99$ in all $60$ held-out runs, with a mean fidelity of $0.996886$. 1080 circuit-noise cells and 6480 confidence-coverage rows are covered by fixed-circuit robustness validation without a locked soundness violation. We then address architectural fairness at $n=16$ using three new studies. In a 120-run exact-gradient multistart diagnostic, MERA has higher fidelity in 58/60 paired restarts and lower long-range error in 60/60, although no run met the prespecified stationarity criterion. Finally, a causal cone-complete, parameter matched local circuit achieves $2.62\times$ greater aggregate gate exposure yet loses all 30 paired comparisons in fidelity, long-range error, energy, and entropy.
summary: This work introduces a 'terminal-register certification' framework to reliably reconstruct complex quantum states, like those from the Ising model, using limited measurement data. By developing rigorous mathematical identities and finite-shot bounds, the authors demonstrate that the MERA ansatz provides a superior, verifiable method for capturing long-range entanglement compared to simpler tensor network or local circuit models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of learning structured quantum states from finite measurement data while ensuring the operational certificate remains meaningful despite measurement imperfections and finite sampling.
main_result: They establish a 'terminal-register certification' protocol, demonstrating that MERA provides a resource-qualified advantage over MPS and local circuits for reconstructing long-range quantum structure in the near-critical regime.
method: The core method involves developing an exact identity relating reconstruction fidelity to the top state fidelity and the terminal measurement probability, coupled with finite-shot confidence bounds.
model_or_system: The study focuses on pure one-dimensional quantum states, specifically using the inverse binary MERA ansatz to represent the ground state of the open-boundary transverse field Ising model.
key_observables: Reconstruction fidelity (F), conditional top state fidelity (F_top), long-range connected-ZZ error, half-chain-entropy error, and energy density error.
important_parameters: The number of qubits (e.g., $n=8, n=16$), the number of simulated training measurements ($560$ million), and confidence parameters ($\delta_D, \delta_T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the causal-discard condition and assumes a calibrated total variation implementation budget is applied to the finite shot certificate to maintain soundness.
figures_summary: The notes summarize comparisons across multiple diagnostic tests, including held-out performance metrics (Table 8 & 10) and paired difference analyses ($\Delta F, \Delta ELR$) comparing MERA against MPS and local circuits (Table 9 & 11).
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the fundamental identity for reconstruction fidelity, deriving finite-shot confidence bounds for both the global failure event and the top state fidelity, and finally applying this framework to compare MERA against competing architectures (MPS, local circuits) on the TFIM ground state.
why_interesting: The rigorous development of operational certificates that account for finite measurements is crucial for translating theoretical quantum simulation power into practical, verifiable quantum computation protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Locked n = 8 held-out evaluation. Every run exceeds the fidelity gate. Orange certificate points identify the six runs above the prespecified 0.01 warning threshold; these are certificate non-tightness observations, not reconstruction failures.

Figure 2: Fixed-circuit robustness validation. Exact terminal distribution shifts remain below their conservative calibrated budgets. The validation covers implementation soundness, not convergence of training under noise.
Figure 3: Eight-qubit architecture comparison. MPS is slightly better than MERA in fidelity, whereas removing MERA disentanglers to obtain TTN causes a pronounced degradation.

Figure 4: Approximately matched aggregate SU(4)-shot-gate exposure. Points show fieldwise means over ten paired replicates; the response is not assumed monotone. At the largest exposure, fidelity is unresolved while long-range error favors MERA-PM225.

Figure 5: Top: exact-gradient 20-restart diagnostic; error bars summarize restart variation and do not certify global optimality. Bottom: the causal-cone-complete local control, which has equal coordinates and greater aggregate gate exposure than MERA-PM225.
